t: Exam Room — Seating by Maximum Distance
o: We maintain a row of $n$ seats and must support `seat()` (place a student at the seat maximizing distance to the nearest occupied seat, ties broken by lowest index; seat 0 if empty) and `leave(p)` (remove the student at p). In the example with n=10: first student takes 0, second compares 0 vs 9 (both distance 1 from an edge... actually 9 gives distance 9 from 0, better than any middle), third finds seat 4 (distance 4 to both neighbors), fourth finds seat 2, then after leaving 4 the next best is 5. Since n can be up to 10^9 we cannot allocate an array of seats — we only track *occupied* positions, of which there are at most ~10^4.
k: Never materialize all n seats; track only the sorted set of occupied indices.

For each adjacent pair of occupied seats (a,b), the best new seat is the midpoint with distance (b-a)/2; also consider edges: seat 0 (distance to first occupant) and seat n-1 (distance to last occupant).
Ties break toward the lower seat index, so compare candidates carefully.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force over All Seats
a.i: Keep a boolean array of size n. For each `seat()` call, scan every seat, compute its distance to the closest occupied seat (or edges when no one sits on that side), and pick the maximum with lowest index. Simple and obviously correct, but O(n) per call is too slow for n = 10^9 in the worst case, though it passes if total work stays small for small n.
s: Store occupancy in a boolean array of length n.
On seat(): if empty room return 0; else for each free seat compute min(distance to left neighbor or i+1 if none, distance to right neighbor or n-i if none).
Track the seat with maximum such distance, preferring smaller index on ties.
a.t: O(n) per seat() call — scanning every seat and its nearest neighbor; leave() is O(1).
a.sp: O(n) for the occupancy array — infeasible for n up to 10^9 in memory-tight settings.

a.n: Approach 2: Sorted Set of Occupied Seats (Optimal)
a.i: Keep occupied seats in a sorted container. The optimal seat always lies either at index 0, at index n-1, or exactly at the midpoint of some gap between consecutive occupants. For each gap (a,b) the candidate is (a+b)/2 with distance (b-a)/2 (floor division handles odd gaps correctly since ties go to the lower seat). Compare edge candidates (distance = position of first/last occupant) against all midpoints and take the best, breaking ties by smaller seat. Each operation costs O(k log k) where k is the number of seated students (at most 10^4), independent of n.
s: Maintain a sorted set (TreeSet / std::set / sorted list) of occupied seat indices.
seat(): if the set is empty, insert and return 0.
Consider candidate 0 with dist = first element, and candidate n-1 with dist = n-1-last element.
For each consecutive pair (a,b), consider mid = (a+b)//2 with dist = (b-a)//2; keep the candidate with max dist, tie-break by smaller seat.
leave(p): remove p from the set.
a.t: O(k log k) per operation where k is the number of seated students (k <= 10^4): set insertion/removal dominates; JavaScript uses linear insertion into a sorted array, still fine for k <= 10^4.
a.sp: O(k) for storing occupied seats only — independent of n, so n = 10^9 is handled easily.

w: In an interview, present Approach 2 directly after sketching the brute force: the key observation is that candidates are only seat 0, seat n-1, and midpoints of gaps between consecutive occupants. Common pitfalls: forgetting the edge candidates (seating at 0 or n-1 can beat every midpoint), mishandling odd-length gaps (use floor division — e.g., gap (0,5) gives seat 2 with distance 2, matching the example's answer of 2 before seat 4 was taken... verify with the sample), and tie-breaking (strictly greater comparison keeps the earlier/lower candidate). Edge cases: single seat (n=1), empty room, leave() then re-seat merging two gaps. Follow-ups: support streaming seat/leave efficiently with a heap of gaps plus lazy deletion, or handle dynamic n.
